newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU's Santer critical of U.S. over aerospace.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU's Santer critical of U.S. over aerospace.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer said on Tuesday that direct United States government interference in favour of civil and military export sales could severely distort the global aerospace market.
Santer, saying there had been regular charges that Washington had resorted to this sort of practice, said this was against rules laid down by the World Trade Organisation.

"We will continue to counteract this whenever the problem arises and, in the longer term, try to persuade the United States to forego such government pressures altogether," Santer told a conference on the future of Europe's aerospace industry.
He did not give details to back up his charge of U.S. government interference in the aerospace market, a high-technology industry forecast to grow rapidly.
But Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) President Manfred Bischoff, also noting strong U.S. funding support for its industry, accused Washington of using its muscle to boost sales.

"The U.S. administration is exploiting its political clout to promote commercial and military aerospace sales -- with the president as the top salesman and the U.S. embassies as local marketing headquarters," Bischoff told the conference.

Several speakers at the symposium referred to the competitive disadvantage of the European aerospace industry -- which has lost 100,000 jobs in a decade -- compared with its U.S. rivals, which they said received key government backing.

Santer said the European Commission was increasingly concerned by the level of indirect subsidies to the U.S. industry through the space agency NASA and huge military research programmes carried out by the civil sector.
"We are continuing to monitor this carefully. We may have to consider re-orienting some of our own strategic approaches in the future if this trend continues," Santer said.
The U.S. aerospace industry dominates world markets with double the European industry's annual turnover of 35 billion European currency units ($44.3 billion) in 1995.

Despite a 30 percent market share in civilian aircraft, Europe's aerospace industry struggles with structural problems, worsened by the fall in defence spending after the Cold War and the slump in orders for civilian aircraft in the early 1990s.
"While the European military market is largely open to competition, the much bigger U.S. market is virtually closed to products from outside the U.S.," DASA's Bischoff said.
Of even greater importance for the American advantage was the "strong and effective partnership the U.S. aerospace industry has established with the public authorities."
"The joint intent is to increase the U.S. industry's lead in the global marketplace," he said, adding Washington had recently proposed a "quantum leap" in government funding.
"All this has resulted in massively government-funded American technology, which is an ever increasing competitive advantage for the American industry," Bischoff said.
U.S. public investment in industry's research and technology was running at about four times the level in Europe, according to Raul Herranz de Miguel, head of Spanish aerospace firm CASA.

"Although industry is investing heavily using its own resources, it cannot hope to stay in the technology race with its main competitor unless there is strong financial support from European governments similar to the one enjoyed by the U.S industry from its government," he said. (1$=0.78 Ecus)
